query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: During high‐temperature exposure, the degradation of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 is governed by the selective, diffusion‐controlled oxidation (or, under reducing conditions, non‐protective reduction) of reactive elements (notably Al and Ti) at high‐energy sites such as grain boundaries and residual defect aggregates. This leads to the formation of a discontinuous, brittle oxide (or reduced) layer that compromises intergranular cohesion and, in combination with residual stresses, triggers the rapid coalescence of microcracks culminating in catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐built AM specimens of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 displaying a single-phase FCC matrix with high dislocation density, refined grains, and process‐induced compositional inhomogeneities at grain boundaries.
generation.intervention: Expose identical specimens to controlled elevated temperatures (e.g., 850–950 °C) in two different gas atmospheres: one oxidizing (with controlled oxygen partial pressure) and one reducing, while keeping all other processing parameters constant.
generation.conditions: Temperature range of 850–950 °C, exposure durations sufficient to develop measurable surface and internal scale features (e.g., 50–100 hours), and gas atmospheres with well‐controlled oxygen (or reducing species) levels.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries and defect sites that act as fast diffusion pathways for Al and Ti, mediating the nucleation and growth of brittle oxide (or nonprotective reduced species) layers.
generation.mechanism: Under oxidizing conditions, Al and Ti diffuse rapidly along high-energy grain boundary networks to form a thin, discontinuous alumina/titania-based oxide scale; however, process-induced residual stresses and compositional fluctuations prevent the formation of a uniform, adherent protective layer. Under reducing conditions, similarly high-diffusivity regions may instead promote internal void formation or inadequate passivation. In both cases, the compromised intergranular integrity leads to early microcrack nucleation and propagation, resulting in rapid, catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-built baseline, specimens exposed to oxidizing gas will show localized continuous oxide layers along grain boundaries with associated microcrack formation, while those in reducing environments will display either internal voids or less protective interfacial films. In both cases, mechanical testing (e.g., fracture toughness, tensile ductility) will reveal significant degradation relative to the pristine state, and catastrophic failure will be preceded by observable intergranular damage.
generation.baseline: The as-built AM alloy exhibits a homogeneous single-phase FCC microstructure with minimal oxidation or microcrack formation, and retains its baseline mechanical performance.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is expected to dominate at elevated temperatures (850–950 °C) and under gas atmospheres with oxygen concentrations (or reducing potential) sufficient to drive the fast diffusion and reaction kinetics along grain boundaries, while below these temperatures or under inert atmospheres the degradation should be minimal.
generation.uncertainty: The precise kinetics of Al and Ti diffusion and the detailed composition and morphology of the oxide/reduced phases are not fully known; additionally, the role of any subtle phase transformations induced by the AM process may further modify the rate and extent of degradation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a statistically significant set of AM specimens and subject them to identical thermal exposures (850–950 °C for 50–100 hours) under two controlled atmospheres: an oxidizing environment (with a fixed oxygen partial pressure) and a reducing environment. After exposure, perform detailed microstructural characterization (using SEM, TEM, and EBSD) to assess the extent and morphology of oxide or reduced phase formation along grain boundaries and within the bulk. Complement the structural analysis with mechanical tests (e.g., tensile, fracture toughness) to quantify degradation.
measurements: Quantitative assessment of oxide/reduced scale thickness and continuity (via SEM/TEM imaging)
Measurement of crack density and location (emphasis on grain boundary versus intragranular)
Fracture toughness and tensile ductility comparisons relative to as-built specimens
Elemental mapping (e.g., EDS) to detect depletion of Al/Ti near degraded regions
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the exposed specimens (both in oxidizing and reducing atmospheres) do not show statistically significant differences in intergranular degradation features (such as oxide scale formation, voids, or microcrack density) compared to the as-built baseline, and if their mechanical properties remain essentially unchanged, then the hypothesis that selective intergranular reactions drive catastrophic failure is falsified.

Oxidation Behavior of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 High-Entropy Alloy Powder

Abstract: One of the most promising applications of FeNiCoCrMoAl-based high-entropy alloy is the fabrication of protective coatings. In this work, gas-atomized powder of FeNiCoCrMo0.5Al1.3 composition was deposited via high-velocity oxygen fuel spraying. It was shown that in-flight oxidation of the powder influences the coating’s phase composition and properties. Powder oxidation and phase transformations were studied under HVOF deposition, and during continuous heating and prolonged isothermal annealing at 800 °C. Optical and scanning electron microscopy observation, energy dispersive X-ray analysis, X-ray diffraction analysis, thermogravimetric analysis, differential thermal analysis, and microhardness tests were used for study. In a gas-atomized state, the powder consisted of BCC supersaturated solid solution. Enhanced Oxidation Resistance of Ultrafine-Grain Microstructure AlCoCrFeNi High Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThis work investigates the effect of ultrafine-grain microstructure on the oxidation behavior of AlCoCrFeNi high entropy alloy (HEA). The ultrafine-grain microstructure is obtained using stationary friction processing performed at two different rotational speeds, 400 and 1800 rpm, for 5 min duration. Processed samples demonstrate high depth of refinement (DOR) and ultrafine grain size (0.43–1 μm) at high rotational speeds along with significant phase transformations from BCC/B2 to FCC microstructure. Further, surface free energy of the ultrafine-grain microstructure is enhanced up to 35%. Oxidation kinetics of the ultrafine-grained sample is decelerated up to 12–48% in a temperature range of 850–1050 °C for a duration of 100 h. Chromia and alumina were the predominant oxides formed in almost all the samples oxidized at elevated temperature. In addition, spinel Co(Cr,Fe)2O4/Fe(Co,Cr)2O4 formation is also detected in the unprocessed oxidized samples.
